tagline: Limestone fences and folk art line a highway through the Smoky Hills.
intro: The Post Rock Scenic Byway winds through fields, pastures and prairie in the Smoky Hills between Lucas and Wilson. Kansas Tourism describes an 18-mile drive through weathered bedrock, with nearly half the route beside Wilson Lake. K-232 carries the Kansas Department of Transportation’s scenic-byway designation; Kansas Tourism highlights the limestone fence posts and the area’s folk art. The dam crossing gives views of the Fencepost limestone bluffs of the Blue Hills along the Saline Valley.

The highway began in 1961 as the link between Interstate 70 and what was then U.S. 40. The rest of its route followed over the next two years. Its byway name reaches further back, to settlers who used local limestone for fencing and construction where wood was scarce. Workers drilled the exposed stone and drove wedges into the holes to split off posts.

Starting at Lucas, follow K-232 south from K-18 through rural land to Wilson Dam. The road crosses the top of the dam, then follows the lake’s eastern shore. Continue through agricultural land and across Interstate 70 to Wilson, where the highway ends at old U.S. 40. In Wilson, Kansas Tourism’s route ends with the World’s Largest Czech Egg.

moments.title: Garden of Eden, Lucas
moments.text: The Garden of Eden’s log cabin is made of limestone: its twelve rooms sit within stone “logs” quarried near Wilson Lake. Samuel P. Dinsmoor, a Union Army veteran who later farmed, retired in 1905 and began working as a sculptor. He spent the rest of his life creating the garden. Its concrete figures express his Populist politics and religious convictions. One figure, Labor Crucified, is surrounded by a doctor, lawyer, preacher and capitalist. A mausoleum in a corner of the lot holds the coffins of Dinsmoor and his first wife, Frances.

moments.title: Carved fence posts
moments.text: Four stone fence posts near Lucas carry the faces of four Lucas residents, carved by California sculptor Fred Whitman. The posts stand in fences along the byway. The material had a practical life before becoming portraiture: settlers quarried the shallow limestone bed for buildings, bridges and fence posts. Freshly exposed stone is soft enough to work, then hardens as it dries in the open air. Quarry workers drilled lines of holes and hammered wedges into them to split off posts. The rough quarry finish usually leaves those drill holes visible in the stone.
moments.notice: Look for the faces carved into four stone posts near Lucas.

moments.title: Wilson Dam
moments.text: K-232 crosses the top of Wilson Dam, a 5,600-foot earth-fill embankment. The reservoir’s original purposes included irrigation, but the Saline River’s salty water made that use unfeasible. The Bureau of Reclamation transferred management and operation of the project to the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers. The Corps designed and built the dam, completing it in 1964, and continues to manage the reservoir. The river enters the lake from the west and leaves it to the east. The Corps manages the lake for flood control, recreation, wildlife and improved downstream water quality.
